units.title: Exposure Ninja's sales process example

claim.text: The source describes Exposure Ninja's sales process as a free website and marketing review, then a follow-up consultation, then a plan, then another follow-up consultation, then becoming a client; the process has been refined over eight years.
claim.quote: our Exposure Ninja sales process is the free website and marketing review. You go through that. We then have a follow-up consultation. We put together a plan. You have a follow-up consultation and then you become a client. And that's the process that we use and that's the kind of framework that this is based on. and we've worked on that process over the last eight years.

units.title: Exposure Ninja's early call-based reviews

claim.text: Exposure Ninja first did website and marketing reviews over a call because they didn't know what the reviews needed to include to make people become a lead; the calls let them learn what feedback people had, where people were, and the appropriate technical level.
claim.quote: when we first started doing our website and marketing reviews, we did them over a call because we didn't know what those reviews needed to include in order to make people become a lead. So, we did them over a call so we could find out um what feedback people had, where people were at, and the sort of level that we needed to put these reviews at.

units.title: Make software trial onboarding painless, fun, and step-by-step

claim.text: The source says offering a trial of a full product can risk losing users because the user must invest time to get the software up and running and may be daunted by the enormity of setup, not because the software is wrong; it recommends making onboarding as painless and ideally as fun as possible, game-like or very step-by-step, so users feel a strong sense of completion, and not giving massive homework straight away.
claim.quote: if you offer a trial of a full product and someone looks in it and they're like, "Oh, this is going to take us ages." You risk losing that person, not because your software is not right, but because the enormity of the task hits them. So it's worth thinking about how you can make the onboarding process of your software as painless as possible and ideally as fun as possible, so they actually feel kind of almost addicted and and it's it's like a game. and there's some kind of game element um or it's very very step by step so they feel a strong sense of completion as they're moving through the process. units.title: Infusionoft setup fee versus Zoho free trial example

claim.text: The source gives a CRM example: Infusionoft charges a setup fee before sale plus monthly fee, not because onboarding costs that much but because the user becomes invested and committed to setup; Zoho offers a free trial to play around with everything, but Exposure Ninja tried Zoho and was put off by the free trial. The source concludes it is about understanding your audience and testing each option to see which works best for you.
claim.quote: You'll have a company like Infusionoft that will charge a setup fee. So they'll charge a large amount of money before the sale and then they'll charge you a monthly fee as well. So why are they doing this? Well, they're charging you that fee not because it cost them a load of money to on board you, but because you've then invested and you're more committed to going through the process of getting the thing set up. Whereas other companies like Zoho will offer you a free trial where you can get in and you can play around with everything. Now, on the surface, you'd say, "Hey Zoho, that's a much better approach." But hey, we use Infusionoft and we've tried Zoho and we got completely put off by the um the free trial. So, you know, it's all about understanding your audience and testing each option and seeing which works best for you.
